title: The passive back-rank defence
summary: Against a knight's or rook's pawn, waiting on the first rank is enough. Against the others, only with the pawn already on the seventh.
part.wait.title: Knight's pawn: wait
part.wait.summary: King in front of the pawn and rook on the first rank: against a knight's pawn, that is enough.
part.corner.title: On the check, the corner
part.corner.summary: Against Black's only trick, the check beside the king, the king goes to the corner, never outwards.
part.rookPawn.title: Rook's pawn and stalemate
part.rookPawn.summary: With a rook's pawn the king lives in the corner, and sometimes having no moves saves the game.
part.kingFirst.title: King first
part.kingFirst.summary: To reach the defence, the king gets in front of the pawn first; the rook waits.
part.home.title: Back home
part.home.summary: The rook returns to the first rank, but never via the corner, which belongs to the king.
part.bishop.title: Bishop's pawn: the same defence loses
part.bishop.summary: One more file on the other side of the king, and the attacking rook threatens mate.
part.active.title: Getting out in time
part.active.summary: Against a bishop's or central pawn, the rook leaves the first rank before the attacking king gets in: to the far end, or to the third rank if the pawn is still on the fourth.
part.seventh.title: Pawn on the seventh, and recap
part.seventh.summary: With the pawn one step from queening, the rook watches the queening square from afar. And the rules to take away.
step.t_knight: A knight's pawn on the third rank, the black king beside it, and no time left for the Philidor defence. Your king is in front of the pawn and the rook on the first rank. What do you play, and why is that enough?
step.t_knight.hint1: Think about where the black rook would need to go to threaten mate on the first rank, and how much room it has for that.
step.t_knight.hint2: Count the files on the other side of your king. If the black rook has no way round, does your rook need to do anything?
step.room: When there is no time to set up the Philidor defence, the most modest one is left: the king in front of the pawn and the rook on the first rank. Against a knight's pawn it is enough. To threaten mate, the black rook would need to reach the first rank on the other side of your king, and there is only the h-file there: no room. So your rook just shuffles along the first rank, 1.Rc1, and nothing changes. This is the position John Emms uses to explain this defence, with colours reversed.
step.naka: Masters know this defence by heart. Carlsen against Nakamura, Sinquefield Cup, Saint Louis, 2017. After a long manoeuvre, Carlsen won the h-pawn and Nakamura took the e-pawn: rook and knight's pawn against rook were left, and the white king reached h6. Nakamura defends with Black, the king on g8, in front of the pawn.
step.naka.m1: 93...Re6+. A check from the side before going home: either the white king steps away from the pawn, or the pawn advances to block.
step.naka.m2: 94.g6. Carlsen blocks with the pawn. Now he threatens 95.Ra8+, and the black king would have no escape: f7 and h7 belong to the pawn.
step.naka.m3: 94...Re8, the only move. The rook returns to the back rank and covers the checking square. It is the defence from the start of this chapter, with colours reversed, and the game was drawn right there.
step.wait: Now you. Wait with the rook on the first rank. Black will bring the king to h3 and push the pawn.
step.wait.hint: Stay on the first rank: 1.Rc1, 2.Rb1, 3.Rc1. If the pawn goes to g2, your king is already on g1.
step.wait.done: Even the pawn's advance changes nothing: your king blocks it on g1, and the rook keeps waiting.
step.t_trick: The black rook has checked on g2. Your king has two squares. Which one draws, and what happens on the other?
step.t_trick.hint1: After your move, see whether the black king can get in front of the pawn.
step.t_trick.hint2: On f1, which square is left free for the black king?
step.corner: In the corner, the king takes h2 away from the black king, and the rook on g2 has nothing to do: it must leave, and the king returns to g1. On f1 it is the opposite: h2 is free, the black king enters, stands beside the pawn and covers g1.
step.cornerDemo: The right way, move by move.
step.cornerDemo.m1: 1.Kh1, to the corner. Now the black king has no h2, and the rook on g2 threatens nothing.
step.cornerDemo.m2: 1...Rh2+. One more check, from the h-file. The black rook had to leave g2.
step.cornerDemo.m3: 2.Kg1. The king returns in front of the pawn, and Black is back where they started.
step.fOne: Now the mistake, so you see why it loses. This step is seen from Black's side.
step.fOne.m2: 1...Kh2! The black king enters through the square your king gave up and covers g1, the queening square.
step.fOne.m3: 2.Rb3. Waiting no longer helps: the pawn is ready to advance with its king beside it.
step.fOne.m4: 2...Rf2+. The check, protected by the pawn, pushes your king further from g1.
step.fOne.m5: 3.Ke1, the only square: g1 belongs to the black king and e2 to the rook.
step.fOne.m6: 3...g2. The pawn will queen with its king beside it and yours cut off: it is the road to the Lucena position, on the losing side.
step.pragg: Seven years later, Carlsen ran into this defence again. Carlsen against Praggnanandhaa, Norway Chess, Stavanger, 2024. In the final trade, Pragg took the f-pawn with check and the white king took the g6-pawn: rook and knight's pawn against rook were left. It is Black's move, and their rook is off the back rank.
step.pragg.m1: 72...Rf8! The only drawing move: the rook returns to the back rank before the check on a8.
step.pragg.m2: 73.Rg7+. This chapter's trick, seen from the other side: a check beside the king.
step.pragg.m3: 73...Kh8. The corner. Here it was the only move, because f8 holds Black's own rook, and it is the square the rule asks for.
step.pragg.m4: 74.Rh7+. One more check, now from the h-file.
step.pragg.m5: 74...Kg8. The king returns in front of the pawn. The checks lead nowhere; after one more, the game was drawn.
step.trick: Now you, from the start: wait on the first rank and, when the check on g2 comes, choose the king's square.
step.trick.hint: 1.Rc1, 2.Rb1 and, on the check on g2, the king goes to the corner: 3.Kh1. Then it returns to g1.
step.trick.done: Black tried everything there was. Your rook never even left the first rank.
step.t_rookPawn: Now the pawn is a rook's pawn, and your king is still on g1. Where does it go, and what does that square cost it?
step.t_rookPawn.hint1: Remember what the knight's pawn left on the other side of your king. And the rook's pawn, what does it leave?
step.t_rookPawn.hint2: If the pawn reaches h2 with your king out of the corner, what happens?
step.rookPawn: To the corner, in front of the pawn. With a rook's pawn there is no file on the other side of your king: the black rook has nowhere to threaten mate from. And if the pawn reaches the seventh with the king out of the corner, it queens with check. But the corner has a price: there the king has no moves. It looks dangerous, and sometimes it is what saves the game.
step.stalemate: Look at this position. Your king on h1 has no move: g1 is attacked by the pawn, g2 by the black king, and the pawn on h2 is protected. If Black can only answer a check by taking your rook, the capture leaves you without moves: it is stalemate.
step.stale.m1: 1.Rg7+! The rook offers itself with check and attacks the black rook. If the black king steps out of check, you take the rook on g8.
step.stale.m2: 1...Rxg7. The only reply that does not lose the rook, and your king has no move: stalemate, a draw.
step.rookPawnMove: Your turn, in the same position: take the king to its place and wait.
step.rookPawnMove.hint: The corner, in front of the pawn.
step.rookPawnMove.done: The king on h1 blocks the pawn, and the rook waits freely on the first rank. With the king on f1, after 1...h2 only one exact check would still hold.
step.t_kingFirst: Your king is not yet in front of the pawn, and the rook is far from the first rank. Which piece moves first, and where to?
step.t_kingFirst.hint1: If the rook goes to the first rank now, what does the black rook do to your king?
step.t_kingFirst.hint2: A whole file can separate your king from the pawn.
step.kingFirst: King first. It has to get in front of the pawn before the black rook cuts it off along a file. The rook can return to the first rank later; a king that is cut off never gets back.
step.raOne: See, from Black's side, what happens if the rook moves first.
step.raOne.m1: 1.Ra1? The rook goes home, but the king stayed on e1.
step.raOne.m2: 1...Rf7! The black rook cuts your king off on the f-file. It can no longer reach g1 or g2.
step.raOne.m3: 2.Ke2. The king looks for a way through, and the f-file is closed.
step.raOne.m4: 2...Rf5. The rook holds the file, and the black king is free to advance with the pawn. Your king watches from afar.
step.grischuk: Ivanchuk against Grischuk, Linares, 2009. The white king took the h-pawn and Grischuk took the f-pawn: rook and knight's pawn against rook were left, with the pawn on g5. The black king, on f7, is not yet in front of the pawn. Grischuk defends with Black.
step.grischuk.m1: 61...Kg8. King first, to the square in front of the pawn. The rook is still off the back rank, and that is fine.
step.grischuk.m2: 62.Rh1. Ivanchuk takes the rook far away, looking for a file to reach the back rank.
step.grischuk.m3: 62...Ra3. The black rook goes far away too, ready to check from the side along the sixth rank.
step.grischuk.m4: 63.Rb1. The white rook goes to the b-file, eyeing the back rank.
step.grischuk.m5: 63...Ra6+! The check, while the white king is on the sixth rank.
step.grischuk.m6: 64.g6. The pawn blocks the check. Now 65.Rb8+ would be mate: f7 and h7 belong to the pawn.
step.grischuk.m7: 64...Ra8! Only now does the rook return to the back rank, at the last moment and with the only move. Ivanchuk still tried 65.Rb7, and the game was drawn.
step.kingFirstMove: Your turn, in the same position as before: king first, then the rook.
step.kingFirstMove.hint: King to f2 and then g1; the rook last.
step.kingFirstMove.done: King in front of the pawn, rook on the first rank: the defence from the first chapter.
step.t_home: Your rook is at the far end, on the short side, and against a knight's pawn its place is the first rank. Which way does it go back?
step.t_home.hint1: Remember where the king goes when the black rook checks beside it.
step.t_home.hint2: If your rook occupies h1, where does the king hide?
step.behind: With a knight's pawn, the rook behind the pawn does not work: the checks would push your king to the long side. It returns to the first rank, but not via h1. That square belongs to your king: it is the corner it goes to on the check.
step.hOne: See, from Black's side, what happens after 1.Rh1.
step.hOne.m1: 1.Rh1? The rook reaches the first rank, but takes the king's corner.
step.hOne.m2: 1...Ra3! It threatens 2...Ra1, mate: the king has no square, and your rook, on its other side, cannot block.
step.hOne.m3: 2.Kf1. The king leaves the corner to avoid mate.
step.hOne.m4: 2...Kf3. The black king follows and takes e2 and g2 away from your king.
step.hOne.m5: 3.Ke1. The king runs to the long side.
step.hOne.m6: 3...Ra1+. The check sweeps along the rank.
step.hOne.m7: 4.Kd2. The king leaves the first rank.
step.hOne.m8: 4...Rxh1. The rook that took the king's corner falls.
step.homeCheck: And what if the way back is blocked? Now the knight's pawn is on the queenside, and your rook is on the short side, on a8. Via a1 it would take your king's corner, and the black king stands on the c-file.
step.homeCheck.m1: 1.Rc8+! First the check: the black king has to leave the c-file.
step.homeCheck.m2: 1...Kb3. The black king steps aside and stands next to the pawn.
step.homeCheck.m3: 2.Rc1. Now the way back: the rook reaches the first rank via the c-file, and a1 stays free for your king.
step.home: Bring the rook home: along the eighth rank to the a-file, and from there to the first.
step.home.done: Back on the first rank, with h1 free for the king. It is the defence from the start of the lesson.
step.homeCheckMove: Now you, with the way back blocked: get the black king out of the way and bring the rook to the first rank.
step.homeCheckMove.hint: First the check, 1.Rc8+; then the rook comes down the c-file.
step.homeCheckMove.done: First the check, then the way back: the rook reached the first rank and a1 stays free for your king.
step.t_bishop: The same defence, but now the pawn is a bishop's pawn. How do Black win?
step.t_bishop.hint1: Now, how many files are there on the other side of the pawn?
step.t_bishop.hint2: Where would the black rook threaten mate if your king left g1?
step.file: The difference is one file. With the pawn on f3, two files are left on the other side of the pawn, g and h. After the check on g2, the black rook moves over to the h-file and threatens mate on h1, and your king has no corner in front of the pawn to run to.
step.bishopDemo: See, from Black's side, how the defence falls.
step.bishopDemo.m2: 2.Kf1. 2.Kh1 would lose too: against a bishop's pawn, the corner is not in front of the pawn.
step.bishopDemo.m3: 2...Rh2! It threatens 3...Rh1, mate: e2 and g2 belong to the pawn, f2 to the black king.
step.bishopDemo.m4: 3.Kg1. The king goes back to cover h1.
step.bishopDemo.m5: 3...f2+. The pawn advances with check and drives the king off g1.
step.bishopDemo.m6: 4.Kf1, the only square: h1 is in the black rook's sights.
step.bishopDemo.m7: 4...Rh1+. A check on the first rank: when the king moves, the black rook takes yours on a1.
step.aronianEnd: This happens in elite games. Aronian against Duda, an online game, 2024. Aronian traded a pair of rooks and reached this position with White: the passive defence against a bishop's pawn, with the black king already on g3. Watch from Duda's side.
step.aronianEnd.m1: 58.Kh1. Aronian looks for the corner, but against a bishop's pawn it is not in front of the pawn.
step.aronianEnd.m2: 58...Rh2+. The h-file belongs to the black rook.
step.aronianEnd.m3: 59.Kg1. The king goes back to cover h1, and the pawn gains time to advance.
step.aronianEnd.m4: 59...f3. The pawn advances, protected by the king.
step.aronianEnd.m5: 60.Re3. Aronian attacks the pawn, but the black king protects it.
step.aronianEnd.m6: 60...Ra2. The rook goes far away and threatens 61...Ra1+: 62.Re1 is the only move, and 62...Rxe1 is mate. Aronian resigned.
step.aronianFix: Go back two moves. Before the trade, Aronian had a choice. He played 56.Re1, to the first rank, and after 56...Ra2 and the trade on g3 he landed in the lost position. Play the move that draws.
step.aronianFix.hint: Against a bishop's pawn the first rank does not work. Keep the rook active on the e-file, far from the black king.
step.aronianFix.done: With the rook away from the first rank, after the trade it can still check from a distance, and the draw holds.
step.t_free: A bishop's pawn, and the black king has not yet reached the third rank. What do you do with the rook, and where to?
step.t_free.hint1: One more move, and the black king enters on g3.
step.t_free.hint2: To give checks, the rook needs distance.
step.free: This is the position Averbakh and Kopaev use for this rule. The black king is one move from entering on g3: it is time to leave the first rank. With the pawn already on the third rank, the rook goes to the far end, to check from behind; the third rank is no use, because the pawn on f3 blocks it and the rook would not reach g3.
step.activeDemo.m1: 1.Rb8. Far away, on the back rank, ready for the checks.
step.activeDemo.m2: 1...Kg3. The black king enters the third rank, beside the pawn.
step.activeDemo.m3: 2.Rg8+. The check from behind drives the king off g3.
step.activeDemo.m4: 2...Kf4. The king stays near the pawn to protect it.
step.activeDemo.m5: 3.Rf8+. One more check, from behind the pawn.
step.activeDemo.m6: 3...Ke3. The king crosses to the other side of the pawn and keeps protecting it.
step.activeDemo.m7: 4.Re8+. The black king cannot escape the checks and protect the pawn at the same time.
step.active: Leave the first rank while there is time. Rook to the far end, and checks.
step.active.hint: 1.Rb8. When the king enters on g3, 2.Rg8+; then 3.Rf8+.
step.active.done: The black king cannot get in and protect the pawn at the same time. One move later, with the king already on g3, it would be lost.
step.thirdRank: And what if the pawn is still on the fourth rank? Now it is a central pawn, on d4, and the black king is one move from the third rank. Waiting on the first rank loses just the same. But the rook has one more square: the third rank, as in the Philidor defence, because the pawn does not block it yet.
step.thirdRank.m1: 1.Rb3! The rook closes the whole third rank: the black king cannot enter on c3, d3 or e3. To make progress, all Black has left is to push the pawn.
step.thirdRank.m2: 1...d3. The pawn advances, protected by the king, and blocks the third rank. Now it is of no use to the rook.
step.thirdRank.m3: 2.Rb8. The rook goes to the far end. With the pawn on the third, the black king has no shelter left from the checks from behind.
step.thirdRank.m4: 2...Ke3. The king enters the third rank, beside the pawn.
step.thirdRank.m5: 3.Re8+! The only move: the check from behind drives the king away from the pawn.
step.thirdRank.m6: 3...Kf3. The king runs to the other side, and the pawn is left without its protector.
step.thirdRank.m7: 4.Rd8. The rook attacks the pawn from behind, and the black king cannot protect it without being checked again. It is the Philidor defence, set up from the first rank.
step.thirdRankMove: Now you, with the pawn on the fourth: first the third rank; after the push, the far end and the checks.
step.thirdRankMove.hint: 1.Rb3 closes the third rank. After 1...d3, 2.Rb8, and when the king enters, 3.Re8+.
step.thirdRankMove.done: With the pawn on the fourth, the third rank comes first; with it on the third, the far end. It is the same gesture: leave the first rank before the attacking king gets in.
step.t_seventh: Now the pawn is on the seventh, and the black king protects it. Which square is your rook's, and what does it do when the black king moves?
step.t_seventh.hint1: Which square does the pawn need to queen?
step.t_seventh.hint2: The rook has to watch that square without coming within reach of the black king.
step.seventh: With the pawn on the seventh, only one square matters: e1, the queening square. The rook goes there. When the black king goes to d3, the rook has to move, and only b1 works: far away, still seeing e1. On a1 the black rook takes it; on d1 the pawn takes it; and on the short side, on g1, it loses, as you will see now.
step.gOne: See, from Black's side, what happens after 1.Rg1.
step.gOne.m1: 1.Rg1? The rook leaves e1 for the short side, close to your king.
step.gOne.m2: 1...Ra5! The black rook heads for the f-file from far away.
step.gOne.m3: 2.Kf3. Your king stays near the pawn, but there is no saving move any more.
step.gOne.m4: 2...Rf5+. The check on the f-file drives your king away.
step.gOne.m5: 3.Kg4. The king attacks the rook, too late.
step.gOne.m6: 3...Rf1. The black rook, protected by the pawn, stands between your rook and e1, and the pawn queens.
step.seventhMove: This is the position Emms uses for the back-rank defence, with colours reversed. Hold the draw.
step.seventhMove.hint: 1.Re1; when the black king goes to d3, the rook goes far away along the first rank, and returns to e1 when it comes back to d2.
step.seventhMove.done: Three only moves, and the draw: the rook never let go of the queening square.
step.recap: What to take away. One: against a knight's or rook's pawn, king in front of the pawn and rook on the first rank; on the check, the king goes to the corner, and the rook never takes the corner. Two: to get there, king first, then the rook. Three: against a bishop's or central pawn, leave the first rank before the attacking king steps onto the third: to the far end, or to the third rank if the pawn is still on the fourth.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge: wait with the rook on the first rank and, when the check comes, go to the corner.
ex.e10: A bishop's pawn on the fourth rank, the black king beside it, and your rook on the first rank. Can you wait, as against the knight's pawn? Find the draw.
ex.e10.hint: Count how many moves the black king needs to enter the third rank, and remember what happens against a bishop's pawn once it does.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Rc3, and after 1...f3, 2.Rc8; when the king goes to g3, 3.Rg8+. It is the Philidor defence, set up from the first rank. Waiting with the rook on the first rank would lose to the king's advance.
ex.e11: A rook's pawn already on the seventh, and the black rook threatens to come down to the first rank. Where does the king go? Find the draw.
ex.e11.hint: With a rook's pawn the corner is the safest square there is. And if your king ends up with no moves, think about what that could be worth.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Kh1, in front of the pawn. 1.Kf1? loses at once: 1...h1=Q is mate. After 1...Ra3, besides waiting on the first rank (2.Rc1, 2.Rd1, 2.Re1 or 2.Rf1), there is a pretty resource: 2.Rb3+! If the black rook takes, it is stalemate, because your king has no square; if the black king steps out of check, 3.Rxa3 wins the rook. With a rook's pawn, the corner and stalemate work for the defender.
ex.e15: A knight's pawn, the black king beside it on the third rank. Stay on the first rank or go behind the pawn? Find the draw.
ex.e15.hint: Against a knight's pawn, what happens if the black rook checks along the first rank and your rook is not there?
ex.e15.solution: Stay: 1.Rb1 (or 1.Rd1, 1.Re1, 1.Rf1; 1.Kh1 and 1.Rc3+ also hold). Against a knight's pawn the first rank draws. Going to the far end, 1.Rc8?, loses: 1...Ra1+ and the king, with no h2 and no g2, has to go to f2, the long side; the black king enters on h2 and the pawn gets through.
ex.e14: A knight's pawn, but your king is not in front of it yet, and the rook is far from the first rank. Where do you start? Find the draw.
ex.e14.hint: The rook can wait. The king cannot: which square does it need to take away from the black king?
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kf2!, which takes g3 away from the black king; 1.Kf1? allows 1...Kg3 and the black king arrives first. After 1...Rd2+, 2.Kg1! (the pawn's corner). If 2...Kh3, 3.Re3+ or 3.Re1 hold; after 3...g3, 4.Re1, and it is the passive defence from the lesson. King first, rook second.
ex.e16: A central pawn on the seventh, and your king can blockade it. After that, every rook move counts. Find the draw.
ex.e16.hint: The black rook wants to come down to the first rank with check. Your rook has to be on the first rank, but not on just any square of it: think about a rook trade and about the pawn.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Ke1, blockading the pawn; 1.Kd2? loses to 1...e1=Q+: the queen is born with check, protected by the rook on e3. Then the rook dances along the first rank: 1...Rc3 2.Rb1, 2...Ra3 3.Rc1, 3...Rb3 4.Ra1. It never stands on the black rook's file (3...Rxa1+ trades rooks and the pawn queens) nor on d1 (the pawn takes). On any other square of the first rank, the black rook's check is met by capturing it.
key.knight: Against a knight pawn, just wait: the king stands in front of the pawn and the rook shuffles along the first rank. A draw.
key.trick: The one thing to watch: when the black rook gives check, the white king goes to the corner. Running the other way loses.
key.bishop: With a bishop pawn the same waiting loses: on the other side of the pawn there is room for the black rook to go round and threaten mate.
key.seventh: The pawn is one step from promoting, with the black king beside it: the rook still holds from the first rank, but every move has to be exact.
history: This is the simplest defence in rook endings: the king stands on the square where the pawn wants to promote, the rook waits on the back rank and the defender just shuffles back and forth. It has no famous name and no date; it is what is left when the Philidor defence was not set up in time. The danger is that it looks as if it works against everything, and it does not: against rook and knight pawns it draws, but against bishop and central pawns it usually loses. Grandmaster Hovhannes Gabuzyan puts it this way: against the pawns in the middle you need to know Philidor's defence; against those near the edge, the back rank is enough. Knowing the difference saves half a point in a lot of games.
practice: Practical challenge: a knight's pawn, your rook on the first rank and the king in front of the pawn. Wait, and on the check go to the corner. The goal is to draw.
